summary: Heinrich Hettrich worked in linguistics, Indology, and Iranian/Central Asian studies. He studied at Saarland University, Giessen, and Munich. He taught at Saarland, Munich, Salzburg, and Zurich, served at Marburg, and held a chair in comparative linguistics at Würzburg from 1989.

Heinrich Hübschmann was a linguist specializing in Iranian, Central Asian, and Indology fields. He studied at Jena under August Schleicher, Tübingen, Munich under Martin Haug, and Leipzig. He became an associate professor at Leipzig in 1876 and professor at Strasbourg in 1877.

Heinrich Kiepert was a historian and archaeologist who studied at Berlin under August Boeckh and Julius Heinrich Petermann, and at Jena. He led the geographical department at Landes-Industrie-Comptoir (1845–1852) and served as professor of geography at Berlin from 1874.

Heinrich Leberecht Fleischer specialized in Iranian, Central Asian, and linguistic studies. He studied at Leipzig under Gottfried Hermann and in Paris under Silvestre de Sacy and Antoine-Léonard Chézy. After teaching at Kreuzschule, he held the Oriental languages chair at Leipzig from 1836.

Heinrich Lüders was a scholar of Indology, Buddhist studies, and linguistics. He studied at Munich and Göttingen, earning his doctorate under Franz Kielhorn. He held posts at Oxford, Göttingen, Rostock, and Kiel before serving as professor in Berlin (1909–1935).

Heinrich R. Zimmer worked in Indology, philosophy, and religious studies. He studied at the Humboldt University of Berlin under Wilhelm Schulze from around 1909 to 1913, and later held academic posts at Greifswald (c. 1920–1924) and Heidelberg (c. 1924–1938).

Heinrich Rickert was a philosopher who studied at the Humboldt University of Berlin (c. 1884–1885) and the University of Strasbourg (c. 1885–1888). He held academic posts at the University of Freiburg (c. 1891–1915) and Heidelberg University (c. 1916–1932).

Heinrich Rückert worked in the fields of history, archaeology, and linguistics. He held academic posts at the University of Jena from around 1845 to 1852 and at the University of Breslau from around 1852 to 1875.
Heinrich Schliemann was an archaeologist and historian. He pursued studies at the University of Paris from 1866 to 1868 and at the University of Rostock around 1869.

Heinrich Schweizer-Sidler worked in linguistics and Indology. He studied at the University of Zurich under Bernhard Hirzel, Johann Caspar von Orelli, and Hermann Sauppe. He taught at Kantonsschule Rämibühl and became professor of Sanskrit and comparative linguistics at Zurich in 1864.

Heinrich Uhle was an Indologist who completed his Dr. phil. at the University of Leipzig around 1874–1877 under Hermann Brockhaus. He also served as a classical languages teacher at the Kreuzschule from 1868 to 1911.

Heinrich Wenzel specialized in Indology and Tibetology. He studied at Jena, Tübingen, and Leipzig, working under Heinrich August Jäschke, Léon Feer, Georg von der Gabelentz, and Friedrich Max Müller. He completed his habilitation at Leipzig, where he briefly held a post in 1887.

Heinrich Zimmer worked in Indology and linguistics. He studied at Strasbourg, Tübingen, and Berlin under Wilhelm Scherer, Siegfried Goldschmidt, Rudolf von Roth, and Albrecht Weber. He held professorships at Greifswald (1881) and Berlin (1901–1910), as well as posts at Heidelberg and Columbia.

Heinrich von Stietencron was an Indologist and religious studies scholar. He studied at Munich, SOAS London, and Heidelberg. After serving as an assistant at Heidelberg in 1965, he was chairholder at the University of Tübingen from 1973 to 1998.

Heinz Adolf Mode specialized in Indology, archaeology, and Buddhist studies. He studied in Berlin, under G. P. Malalasekera and Otto Fischer, and at the University of Basel. From 1948 to 1978, he was professor of Oriental archaeology at the University of Halle.

Heinz Bechert was an Indology and Buddhist studies scholar. He studied at Munich, Hamburg, and Mainz, learning under Erich Frauwallner and Ernst Waldschmidt. He worked at Saarland and Mainz before serving as Chair of Indology at the University of Göttingen from 1965 to 2000.

Helen Hardacre is a scholar of Japanology and religion. She studied at Vanderbilt and the University of Chicago under Joseph Kitagawa and Jonathan Z. Smith. She held posts at Princeton (1980–1989), Griffith (1990–1992), and Harvard University beginning in 1992.

Helen J. Baroni specializes in Buddhist studies, Japanology, and religious studies. She studied at Columbia University under doctoral supervisor Paul B. Watt and held an academic post at the University of Hawaiʻi (attested 2006).

Helen Wang specializes in history, archaeology, Iranian and Central Asian studies, and sinology. She studied at SOAS University of London and became Curator of East Asian Money in the Department of Coins and Medals at the British Museum around 1993.
Helena Blankleder is a scholar of Tibetology and Buddhist studies who studied under traditional teachers Taklung Tsetrul Pema Wangyal Rinpoche and Jigme Khyentse Rinpoche (both attested 1999).
